topics.title: Sets: definitions and ways of description
topics.content:
Definition of a set

A set is a fundamental mathematical concept that denotes a collection of distinct objects united by some common property. The objects belonging to a set are called elements. If an element a belongs to a set A, we write a ∈ A; otherwise a ∉ A.

Ways to define sets
  • By listing elements: A = {a1, a2, ..., an}. For example, A = {1, 2, 3}.
  • By describing a characteristic property: B = {x | P(x)}, where P(x) is a condition satisfied by the elements. For example, B = {x | x ∈ ℕ, x > 0}.
Empty and universal sets

The empty set ∅ contains no elements. The universal set U contains all elements of the considered domain of discourse.

Subset

A set A is called a subset of B (A ⊆ B) if every element of A is also an element of B. If A ⊆ B and A ≠ B, then A is a proper subset.

Cardinality of a set

The cardinality |A| of a set is the number of its elements (for finite sets). For infinite sets, the notion of countability is introduced.

topics.title: Operations on sets and their properties
topics.content:
Basic operations
  • Union A ∪ B = {x | x ∈ A or x ∈ B} — the set of elements belonging to at least one of the sets.
  • Intersection A ∩ B = {x | x ∈ A and x ∈ B} — the set of elements belonging to both sets.
  • Difference A \ B = {x | x ∈ A and x ∉ B} — elements of A that are not in B.
  • Symmetric difference A ∆ B = (A \ B) ∪ (B \ A) = {x | x ∈ A or x ∈ B, but not both}.
  • Complement A̅ = {x ∈ U | x ∉ A} — all elements of the universe that are not in A.
Properties of operations
  • Commutativity: A ∪ B = B ∪ A, A ∩ B = B ∩ A.
  • Associativity: (A ∪ B) ∪ C = A ∪ (B ∪ C), (A ∩ B) ∩ C = A ∩ (B ∩ C).
  • Distributivity: A ∪ (B ∩ C) = (A ∪ B) ∩ (A ∪ C); A ∩ (B ∪ C) = (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C).
  • De Morgan's laws: (A ∪ B)̅ = A̅ ∩ B̅; (A ∩ B)̅ = A̅ ∪ B̅.
  • Idempotent laws: A ∪ A = A, A ∩ A = A.
  • Absorption laws: A ∪ (A ∩ B) = A, A ∩ (A ∪ B) = A.
  • Properties with empty and universal sets: A ∪ ∅ = A, A ∩ ∅ = ∅, A ∪ U = U, A ∩ U = A.

It is convenient to illustrate operations with Venn diagrams.

topics.title: Binary relations and their properties
topics.content:
Definition

A binary relation between sets A and B is any subset R ⊆ A × B. If (a, b) ∈ R, we write a R b. If A = B, we speak of a relation on the set A.

Properties of relations
  • Reflexivity: ∀a ∈ A: a R a.
  • Irreflexivity: ∀a ∈ A: a R a does not hold.
  • Symmetry: ∀a, b ∈ A: a R b ⇒ b R a.
  • Antisymmetry: ∀a, b ∈ A: (a R b and b R a) ⇒ a = b.
  • Transitivity: ∀a, b, c ∈ A: (a R b and b R c) ⇒ a R c.
Important types of relations
  • Equivalence relation (reflexive, symmetric, transitive) partitions the set into equivalence classes.
  • Order relation (reflexive, antisymmetric, transitive) — partial order. If additionally for any a, b we have a R b or b R a, then it is a linear (total) order.
  • Tolerance relation (reflexive, symmetric) — a weakened equivalence.

Example: the relation "≤" on numbers is a linear order; the relation "divides" on natural numbers is a partial order.

topics.title: Functions (mappings)
topics.content:
Definition

A function (mapping) from set A to set B is a binary relation f ⊆ A × B such that each element a ∈ A is assigned exactly one element b ∈ B. Notation: f: A → B, f(a) = b. A is the domain, B is the codomain.

Types of functions
  • Injection (one‑to‑one mapping): distinct elements of A have distinct images in B (f(a₁) = f(a₂) ⇒ a₁ = a₂).
  • Surjection (onto mapping): every element of B has at least one preimage (∀b ∈ B ∃a ∈ A: f(a) = b).
  • Bijection (one‑to‑one correspondence): both injective and surjective.
Composition and inverse function

The composition of functions (f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x)). The inverse function exists only for bijections.

The cardinality of a set is related to the existence of bijections: two sets have the same cardinality if a bijection exists between them.

topics.title: Combinatorics: basic rules
topics.content:
Combinatorics studies methods for counting the number of combinations of objects.

Sum rule

If an object A can be chosen in n ways, and an object B in m ways, and the choices are disjoint, then choosing "either A or B" can be done in n + m ways.

Product rule

If object A can be chosen in n ways, and after each such choice object B can be chosen in m ways, then the ordered pair (A, B) can be chosen in n·m ways.

Inclusion–exclusion principle

For the union of intersecting sets: |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| - |A ∩ B|. For three sets: |A ∪ B ∪ C| = |A|+|B|+|C| - |A∩B| - |A∩C| - |B∩C| + |A∩B∩C|.

topics.title: Combinatorial configurations: permutations, arrangements, combinations
topics.content:
Consider a set of n distinct elements.

Permutations

The number of ways to order all n elements: P(n) = n! (n factorial). Example: 3! = 6.

Arrangements

Arrangements of n items taken k at a time (k ≤ n) are ordered selections of size k. Number of arrangements: A(n, k) = n! / (n-k)!. Example: how many three‑digit numbers can be formed from the digits 1,2,3,4 without repetition? A(4,3)=24.

Combinations

Combinations of n items taken k at a time are unordered selections (subsets) of size k. Number of combinations: C(n, k) = n! / (k!·(n-k)!). Also denoted as binomial coefficient. Example: number of ways to choose 2 books from 5: C(5,2)=10.

Properties of combinations
  • C(n, k) = C(n, n-k).
  • Recurrence: C(n, k) = C(n-1, k-1) + C(n-1, k).
  • Binomial theorem: (a + b)ⁿ = Σ_{k=0}^{n} C(n, k) a^{n-k} b^{k}.
Arrangements and combinations with repetitions
  • Arrangements with repetition: A'(n, k) = n^k (order matters, repetition allowed).
  • Combinations with repetition: C'(n, k) = C(n+k-1, k).

topics.title: Graph theory: basic concepts
topics.content:
Definition of a graph

A graph G = (V, E) consists of a set of vertices V and a set of edges E connecting pairs of vertices. An edge may be directed (arc) or undirected. If an edge connects a vertex to itself, it is called a loop.

Degree of a vertex

The degree deg(v) of a vertex is the number of edges incident to it (for undirected graphs). In directed graphs, we distinguish the out‑degree (number of outgoing arcs) and the in‑degree.

A graph is called simple if it contains no loops and no multiple edges.

Types of graphs
  • Complete graph K_n: every pair of vertices is connected by an edge.
  • Bipartite graph: vertices can be split into two parts so that every edge connects vertices from different parts.
  • Tree: a connected graph with no cycles.
  • Directed graph (digraph): all edges are directed.
Path and cycle

A path is a sequence of vertices where each consecutive pair is connected by an edge. A cycle is a path that starts and ends at the same vertex without repeating edges.

Connectivity

A graph is connected if there exists a path between any two vertices. A connected component is a maximal connected subgraph.

topics.title: Special types of graphs and traversal algorithms
topics.content:
Eulerian cycle and path

An Eulerian cycle is a cycle that traverses every edge of the graph exactly once. An undirected graph has an Eulerian cycle if and only if it is connected and every vertex has even degree. An Eulerian path (not a cycle) exists if exactly two vertices have odd degree.

Hamiltonian cycle

A Hamiltonian cycle is a cycle that visits each vertex exactly once. Finding a Hamiltonian cycle is an NP‑complete problem.

Graph traversals
  • Breadth‑first search (BFS): level‑by‑level traversal; used to find the shortest path in an unweighted graph.
  • Depth‑first search (DFS): goes as deep as possible; used to test connectivity, find cycles, topological sorting.
Weighted graphs

Weighted graphs have numerical labels on edges. Dijkstra's algorithm finds the shortest paths from a single source to all other vertices in a graph with non‑negative weights.

topics.title: Trees and their properties
topics.content:
Definition of a tree

A tree is a connected graph with no cycles.

Basic properties
  • A tree with n vertices has exactly n-1 edges.
  • Any two vertices are connected by a unique path.
  • Adding any edge creates a cycle; removing any edge disconnects the graph.
Directed tree

A directed tree is a rooted tree where edges are directed away from the root.

Forest

A forest is a disconnected graph whose components are trees.

Spanning tree

A spanning tree is a subgraph that contains all vertices and is a tree. Algorithms for constructing a minimum spanning tree in a weighted graph: Prim's and Kruskal's algorithms.

Binary trees

Binary trees are used in computer science: each node has at most two children. A binary search tree allows efficient search, insertion, and deletion.

topics.title: Boolean algebra and logical operations
topics.content:
Basic concepts

Boolean algebra is the algebra of logic, operating on variables that can take two values: 0 (false) and 1 (true).

Basic operations
  • Conjunction (AND, ∧): 1 only if both operands are 1.
  • Disjunction (OR, ∨): 0 only if both operands are 0.
  • Negation (NOT, ¬): inverts the value.
  • Implication (→): a → b is equivalent to ¬a ∨ b.
  • Equivalence (↔): a ↔ b is true when a and b are equal.
Truth tables

Truth tables specify the result of an operation for all input combinations.

Laws of Boolean algebra
  • Commutativity: a ∧ b = b ∧ a, a ∨ b = b ∨ a.
  • Associativity: (a ∧ b) ∧ c = a ∧ (b ∧ c), (a ∨ b) ∨ c = a ∨ (b ∨ c).
  • Distributivity: a ∧ (b ∨ c) = (a ∧ b) ∨ (a ∧ c); a ∨ (b ∧ c) = (a ∨ b) ∧ (a ∨ c).
  • De Morgan's laws: ¬(a ∧ b) = ¬a ∨ ¬b; ¬(a ∨ b) = ¬a ∧ ¬b.
  • Absorption laws: a ∧ (a ∨ b) = a; a ∨ (a ∧ b) = a.
  • Laws with constants: a ∧ 0 = 0, a ∧ 1 = a, a ∨ 0 = a, a ∨ 1 = 1.
  • Double negation: ¬(¬a) = a.

Every Boolean function can be represented in DNF (disjunctive normal form) or CNF (conjunctive normal form).

topics.title: Minimization of Boolean functions. Karnaugh maps.
topics.content:
Minimization of Boolean functions yields simpler logic circuits. One of the visual methods is the Karnaugh map (K‑map).

Karnaugh maps

A Karnaugh map for n variables is a table of 2ⁿ cells, each corresponding to one combination of the variables. Cells are arranged so that adjacent cells differ by the value of only one variable (Gray code).

Minimization rules
  • Form rectangular blocks of 1, 2, 4, 8, ... adjacent cells (including cyclic adjacency).
  • The larger the block, the simpler the resulting term.
  • Each block gives the product of variables (or their negations) that do not change within the block.
  • The minimal DNF is obtained as the disjunction of minimal covers of all ones.

Example: for a function of two variables the map is 2×2; for three variables – 2×4; for four – 4×4. Karnaugh maps are convenient for functions of up to 4‑5 variables. For larger numbers, the Quine–McCluskey method is used.

topics.title: Mathematical logic: propositions and predicates
topics.content:
Propositions

A proposition is a statement that can be true or false. Propositional logic deals with simple propositions and connectives (¬, ∧, ∨, →, ↔).

Predicates

A predicate is a function that depends on variables and becomes a proposition when concrete values are substituted. For example, P(x) = "x > 0". The truth set of a predicate is the set of values for which it is true.

Quantifiers
  • Universal quantifier ∀x P(x) — "for all x, P(x) is true".
  • Existential quantifier ∃x P(x) — "there exists x such that P(x) is true".

Formulas of predicate logic are built from predicates, quantifiers, and connectives. An interpretation specifies the domain and the meaning of the predicates.

A valid formula (tautology) is true in every interpretation. A contradiction is false in every interpretation.

Rules for negating quantifiers: ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x); ¬∃x P(x) ≡ ∀x ¬P(x).

topics.title: Recurrence relations and methods for solving them
topics.content:
Definition

A recurrence relation defines a sequence by expressing each term in terms of previous ones. For example, Fibonacci numbers: F₀ = 0, F₁ = 1, Fₙ = Fₙ₋₁ + Fₙ₋₂ for n ≥ 2.

Linear homogeneous recurrence relations

Linear homogeneous recurrence relations with constant coefficients have the form: aₙ = c₁·aₙ₋₁ + c₂·aₙ₋₂ + ... + cₖ·aₙ₋ₖ.

Solution method

Look for a solution of the form aₙ = rⁿ. Substituting gives the characteristic equation rᵏ = c₁·rᵏ⁻¹ + ... + cₖ. The roots r₁,...,rₖ give the general solution aₙ = α₁·r₁ⁿ + ... + αₖ·rₖⁿ (if the roots are distinct). If there are multiple roots, we multiply by powers of n.

For non‑homogeneous equations, first find a particular solution depending on the form of the non‑homogeneous term, then add it to the general solution of the homogeneous equation.

Example: solve Fₙ = Fₙ₋₁ + Fₙ₋₂. The characteristic equation r² - r - 1 = 0 → roots (1±√5)/2 (the golden ratio).

topics.title: Principle of mathematical induction
topics.content:
Mathematical induction is a method for proving statements that depend on a natural number n.

Simple induction
  1. Base case: prove the statement for n = 1 (or another initial value).
  2. Inductive step: assume the statement holds for n = k (induction hypothesis), then prove it for n = k+1.
Example

Prove that 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n+1)/2.
Base n=1: 1 = 1·2/2 true.
Inductive step: assume true for n, then for n+1: sum = n(n+1)/2 + (n+1) = (n+1)(n/2+1) = (n+1)(n+2)/2.

Strong induction

In the hypothesis we assume the statement holds for all smaller values (e.g., from 1 to k).

Induction is widely used in combinatorics, number theory, and algorithm analysis.

topics.title: Basics of coding theory
topics.content:
Coding is the process of converting information into a form suitable for transmission or storage. A code is a set of codewords (sequences of symbols).

Basic concepts
  • Alphabet — a finite set of symbols (e.g., {0,1} for binary code).
  • Code length — the number of symbols in a codeword.
  • Unique decodability: the code must allow a unique segmentation of a sequence into codewords. Prefix codes (no codeword is a prefix of another) guarantee unique decodability.
Kraft's inequality

For the existence of a prefix code with lengths l₁,...,lₘ over an alphabet of size r, it is necessary and sufficient that Σ r^{-lᵢ} ≤ 1.

Optimal coding

Huffman's algorithm constructs a prefix code with minimum average length for given symbol probabilities.

Error‑correcting codes

Codes with error detection and correction add redundancy. The Hamming distance between two words is the number of positions in which they differ. A code can detect up to d-1 errors and correct up to ⌊(d-1)/2⌋ errors, where d is the minimum Hamming distance between codewords.

Examples: Hamming code (corrects a single error), cyclic codes, Reed–Solomon codes.
